title: Beban House known as one of Nanaimo's most haunted buildings
excerpt: Building has had many ghost sightings since it was built in 1930
content:
Published 5:30 am Tuesday, October 27, 2026

It’s not hard to understand why so many people believe that the old Beban House on Bowen Road is haunted.

The building, which hasn’t seen many changes since it was constructed by Frank and Hannah Beban in 1930, has hidden stairwells, stained-glass windows, narrow hallways and a reputation for being one of Nanaimo’s most haunted places.

There have have been sightings in the basement of a young Chinese boy, said to be a former servant of the Beban family who died on the property, a woman in a white dress who appears in the building’s windows or floating through the upstairs hallways, and other occurrences include faucets turning themselves on and off, doors and windows locking or unlocking by themselves, and disembodied voices or laughter in empty rooms.

Corey Sugiyama, executive director for BGC Central Vancouver Island which is currently leasing the building from the City of Nanaimo, said he has not seen a ghost or experienced paranormal activity since he started working there, but he’s certainly familiar with the stories about the building.

“I don’t know how these stories got started, but there’s a lot of oral history about ghosts and other supernatural incidents in Beban House that have been shared through the community over many years,” he said.

“It’s a very old and unique building, and many different groups and organizations have worked from here for decades, so a lot of people believe they have seen or heard things here that couldn’t be explained.”

Sugiyama said television networks and online shows have been touring the building for years with equipment to detect supernatural activity, and parapsychologists to see if they could find anything unusual about the building.

“Some of them claim to have sensed a presence in some of the rooms,” he said.

“Another group is coming in the new year. Beban House is owned by the city and is a public building, so we try to accommodate them while we continue to work on BGC’s programs.”

Sugiyama said BGC, a non-profit child, youth and family-serving organization, has recognized the potential of working from a building that has a well-known reputation for being haunted.

He said that for the past three Halloweens, BGC has played off the notoriety of the building and has been hosting the annual Haunting of Beban House fundraiser to help pay for its programs.

This year’s Haunting of Beban House took place on Oct. 23-24.

“We’ve had about 500 people attend the event during each of the past two years,” Suguymana said.

“We’ve done a lot of research on the building and its history and we’ve had a lot of antique furniture donated so we could set up the rooms with haunted themes for visitors to tour and enjoy.”

Sugiyama said BGC was also handing out electromagnetic-field detectors that can measure invisible energy waves to visitors at this year’s event, to see if they could pick up any paranormal activity taking place.

“Some of the kids said they were definitely getting fluctuations from their EMF detectors, but I’ve noticed that even a nearby cellphone can set them off,” he said.

“However, who knows? They may actually be detecting ghosts.”
